t.textos.etana.pasajes.2.texto: Paraphrase. The eagle says to Etana: "Put your breast against my breast, hold on to the feathers of my wings and put your arms on my sides". It carries him upward. After one double league it says to him: "Look, my friend, at how the earth is", and Etana sees that the earth looks like a hill and the sea like a stream of water. Higher up, the earth looks like a garden and the sea like a bucket of water or an irrigation ditch. Higher still, Etana can no longer see the earth or the sea. Frightened, he asks the eagle to turn back. In the Nineveh version the eagle carries him as far as the gates of Anu, Enlil and Ea, where they bow down; in another passage they fall toward the earth. The ending has been lost.
t.textos.etana.pasajes.2.fuente: Paraphrase based on Kinnier Wilson (1985), Haul (2000) and Dalley (1989)
t.textos.etana.pasajes.2.nota_academica: The order and number of stages differ between versions, and some images (the sea as a "bucket" or "sheepfold") are read in different ways. The legend was known long before the written poem: Akkadian cylinder seals (c. 2300 BC) show a man carried by an eagle while shepherds and dogs look up. The Sumerian King List sums up Etana as "the one who went up to heaven".
t.textos.etana.pasajes.2.lectura_astrona: In Chariots of the Gods? (1968), Erich von Däniken cites Etana's flight as proof that the ancients described the Earth seen from a great height with an accuracy impossible without flying machines; Sitchin repeats the reading.

That things look smaller from above is an experience within reach of anyone who climbs a mountain or a ziggurat. The text's comparisons are agricultural (garden, ditch, bucket); they show neither curvature nor any feature that would require flight. Flights on birds are a universal mythical motif, and the narrative itself includes a fall and the hero's fear, which fits poorly with a technical flight.
Etana's flight is often cited in histories of aviation and of the space imagination as the oldest surviving account of flight, a precursor of Icarus and of the literature of celestial journeys.
Synthesis of reception; see Stephanie Dalley, Myths from Mesopotamia, 1989 (introduction to Etana)
t.textos.adapa.version: Fragments of four manuscripts: one Middle Babylonian found at El-Amarna (Egypt, 14th century BC, used in the teaching of Akkadian) and three Neo-Assyrian from Ashurbanipal's library (7th century BC)
t.textos.adapa.estructura.0.sinopsis: Introduction of Adapa, sage of Eridu, created by Ea as a model of men, endowed with wisdom but not with eternal life. He serves daily in the temple, prepares Ea's bread and water and fishes for his table.
t.textos.adapa.estructura.1.sinopsis: While he is fishing, the south wind capsizes his boat; Adapa breaks its wing with a curse and the wind stops blowing for seven days. Anu summons him. Ea advises him to dress in mourning, to win over Tammuz and Gizzida at the gate and not to take the bread or the water of death. Anu, calmed, offers him instead the bread and water of life, which Adapa refuses; he is sent back to earth.
t.textos.adapa.estructura.2.sinopsis: Parallel versions of the ending: Anu laughs at Ea and wonders why a man has come to know the secrets of heaven; privileges are fixed for Eridu, and the text ends with an incantation against the illness that the south wind brings to mankind.
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.0.texto:
The south wind […] when
it had (driven) me to the house of my lord, I said:
"O south wind, on the way I will […] you all that
your wing I will break". While he spoke with his mouth,
the wing of the south wind was broken; for seven days
the south wind did not blow upon the land. Anu
called his messenger Ilabrat:
"Why has the south wind not blown upon the land
for seven days?". His messenger Ilabrat answered him: "My lord,
Adapa, the son of Ea, the wing of the south wind
has broken".
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.0.fuente: Spanish version based on R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (1912), pp. 70–71, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.0.nota_academica: The El-Amarna fragment has red dots marking the words, proof that it was used by Egyptian scribes to learn Akkadian. Rogers reconstructs the opening in the first person; today it is understood as a third-person narrative with direct speech by Adapa. "Breaking the wing" of the wind is an effective curse: Izre'el has shown that the whole story revolves around the power of the word. The south wind (šūtu) brought the storms of the Persian Gulf.
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.0.lectura_astrona: Robert Temple (The Sirius Mystery, 1976) identifies Adapa with Oannes, the amphibious being who according to Berossus came out of the sea to teach civilization, and considers him an extraterrestrial visitor from Sirius, linking him with supposed astronomical knowledge of the Dogon people of Mali. Sitchin, for his part, sees in Adapa's journey to heaven an ascent to an Anunnaki ship.

In the lists of sages (apkallū), Adapa appears as a human sage of Eridu and, in some, he is associated with U-an (Oannes) as the first of the seven antediluvian apkallū; the reliefs that show them in a "fish suit" represent priests or protective genies dressed in fish skin, a ritual figure. Walter van Beek's fieldwork (1991) among the Dogon did not find the knowledge about Sirius that Temple attributed to them, which came from Griaule's ethnography. Adapa's journey is a summons before Anu's court, told in the language of the court.
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.1.texto:
"[…] When you stand before Anu,
bread of death they will set before you:
do not eat. Water of death they will set before you:
do not drink. Garments they will set before you:
put them on. Oil they will set before you: anoint yourself.
The counsel I have given you, do not forget it. The words
that I have spoken to you, hold fast to them".
[…]
"Why has Ea revealed to impure mankind
the heart of heaven and of earth? A heart […]
he has created in him, he has made him a name.
What can we do with him? Bread of life
bring him, that he may eat". Bread of life
they brought him, but he did not eat. Water of life
they brought him, but he did not drink. Garments
they brought him; he put them on. Oil
they brought him; he anointed himself.
Anu looked at him; he marveled (?) at him.
"Come, Adapa, why have you not eaten, not drunk?
(Now) you shall not live. […] mankind […]". "Ea, my lord,
said: 'Do not eat, do not drink'".
"Take him and return him to his land".
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.1.fuente: Spanish version based on R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (1912), pp. 74–76, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.1.nota_academica: A central and much-debated passage: did Ea deceive Adapa so that he would not obtain immortality, or did he misjudge Anu's reaction? Or would the "bread of life" have been deadly for a man? Rogers already compared it with the tree of life of Genesis 3. Today the line is translated "why has Ea revealed to a useless (or impure) man the secrets of heaven and earth?". The line "you shall not live" is sometimes understood as "alas for weak mankind!". The food and water of life also appear in the Descent of Inanna.
t.textos.adapa.pasajes.1.lectura_astrona: For Sitchin, the "bread and water of life" are a longevity treatment specific to the Anunnaki, which Enki would have wanted to deny his human son so that humans would not attain the long life of their creators.

The story belongs to a series of Mesopotamian myths about lost immortality (Gilgamesh and the plant, Etana and the plant of birth) that explain why man, though wise, is mortal. Bread, water, garments and oil are the usual gifts of hospitality at court; offering food to a guest in Anu's heaven integrated him into the divine world.
Shlomo Izre'el reads the myth as a reflection on language: Adapa breaks the wing of the wind with a word and loses eternal life by obeying another word. The text, used to teach Akkadian, would show that language has power over life and death.
Shlomo Izre'el, Adapa and the South Wind: Language Has the Power of Life and Death, 2001
t.textos.erra-ishum.version: Akkadian poem in 5 tablets (about 750 lines), composed by Kabti-ilani-Marduk probably in the 8th century BC (other proposals: 11th–9th centuries); Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian copies from Assur, Nineveh, Sultantepe, Babylon and Ur
t.textos.erra-ishum.estructura.0.sinopsi: Invocation to Marduk and Ishum. Erra, god of war and plague, lies lethargic on his bed. The Sebettu (Seven), his divine weapons, incite him to war. Ishum, his counselor, tries to calm him. Erra goes to Babylon and persuades Marduk to leave his throne to renew his image and his insignia, promising to look after the world in his absence.
t.textos.erra-ishum.estructura.1.sinopsi: Marduk goes down to the Underworld and dire omens occur. Erra seizes power and decides to destroy; the gods are afraid. Ishum tries to dissuade him.
t.textos.erra-ishum.estructura.2.sinopsi: Erra unleashes destruction: he announces that he will annihilate the land, the righteous and the wicked. Ishum laments the catastrophe.
t.textos.erra-ishum.estructura.3.sinopsi: Ishum tells Erra what he has caused: civil war in Babylon, the sack of Uruk, Sippar, Der; the father buries the son. Ishum attacks Mount Sharshar and destroys his enemies, which appeases Erra.
t.textos.erra-ishum.estructura.4.sinopsi: Erra, calmed, acknowledges his fury and blesses Ishum. The recovery of Babylon and the submission of the Suteans are announced. Colophon: the poem was revealed in a dream to Kabti-ilani-Marduk and serves as an amulet against plague in the houses where it is kept.
t.textos.erra-ishum.pasajes.0.texto: Paraphrase. Ishum reproaches Erra: "Warrior Erra, you have killed the righteous and the unrighteous, the one who sinned against you and the one who did not sin". He describes how the inhabitants of Babylon, who were like birds in their nest, took up arms and turned against one another; the furious governor ordered the city to be sacked; the enemy desecrated the temples of Uruk, the city of Ishtar's prostitutes; Der was left desolate. In the land, the son hates his father and the mother shuts the door on her daughter; whoever did not die in battle dies of plague, and whoever did not die of plague is plundered by the enemy. Erra, on hearing this, is appeased and says that, when he rages, he destroys as if he were any god. At the end, the poem states that it was revealed in a dream to Kabti-ilani-Marduk, who wrote it down without adding or removing a single line, and that in the house where this tablet is kept Erra will do no harm.
t.textos.erra-ishum.pasajes.0.fuente: Paraphrase based on Cagni (1977) and Foster (2005)
t.textos.erra-ishum.pasajes.0.nota_acade: Erra and Ishum is an unusual theodicy: historical chaos (invasions by Suteans and Arameans, civil wars and plague in the Babylon of the early 1st millennium) is explained by the absence of the supreme god and the free rein of a violent god. P. Machinist (1983) analyzed the tension between rest and violence as the key to the poem. The tablets were used as amulets: extracts have been found on tablets pierced so they could be hung up.
t.textos.erra-ishum.pasajes.0.lectura_as: In The Wars of Gods and Men (1985) and The End of Days (2007), Sitchin interprets Erra's "seven weapons" as nuclear weapons with which Nergal (Erra) and Ninurta (Ishum) would have destroyed the Sinai spaceport and the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah around 2024 BC; the radioactive "evil wind" would then have wiped out Sumer.

The Sebettu ("the Seven") are a group of warrior deities, identified with the Pleiades and present in Neo-Assyrian incantations and reliefs as protective figures. The poem describes swords, plunder, civil war and plague, and names Mesopotamian cities (Babylon, Uruk, Sippar, Der), not the Sinai. The end of Ur III came around 2004 BC through the Elamite conquest and an economic crisis documented in the letters of Ibbi-Sin and in the Sumerian laments; there is no trace of radioactivity in the sediments.
t.textos.erra-ishum.pasajes.0.lectura_ac: The poem is read today as a reflection on collective violence and trauma: it describes civil war from the point of view of the victims (the father who buries his son) and acknowledges, through the god's own mouth, the irrationality of violence, something rare in ancient religious literature.
Peter Machinist, "Rest and Violence in the Poem of Erra", Journal of the American Oriental Society 103, 1983
t.textos.nergal-ereshkigal.version: Two Akkadian versions: a short Middle Babylonian one found at El-Amarna (14th century BC, about 90 lines), and a much longer Standard Babylonian one from Sultantepe (Huzirina, 7th century BC) and Uruk
The gods hold a banquet and, since Ereshkigal cannot come up, they invite her to send for her share. Her vizier Namtar goes up to heaven; all the gods rise before him except Nergal.
Ereshkigal demands that the disrespectful god be handed over to her. Ea advises Nergal: in the Amarna version he gives him fourteen demons to post at the gates; in the Sultantepe version he advises him not to accept a seat, food, drink or a bath in the Underworld and, above all, not to give in to desire.
In Amarna, Nergal throws Ereshkigal down, seizing her by the hair; she offers to marry him and share power. In Sultantepe, Nergal lies with her for six days, escapes, and Ereshkigal threatens to raise the dead if he does not return. Nergal comes back and stays as husband and king of the Underworld.
t.textos.nergal-ereshkigal.pasajes.0.tex:
When the gods prepared a banquet,
to their sister Ereshkigal
they sent a messenger:
"Though we should go down to you,
you could not come up to us;
therefore send (here) and take your portion".
Ereshkigal sent Namtar, her messenger.
[…]
"Do not kill me, my brother. Let me tell you a word".
Nergal listened to her; his hands slackened. She wept and sobbed:
"You shall be my husband; I shall be your wife. I will give you
dominion over the wide earth. I will put the tablet
of wisdom in your hand. You shall be lord,
I shall be lady". When Nergal heard these words,
he took her, kissed her and wiped away her tears:
"What is it that you have wanted of me for months,
until now?".
t.textos.nergal-ereshkigal.pasajes.0.fue: Spanish version based on R. W. Rogers, Cuneiform Parallels to the Old Testament (1912), pp. 131–135, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.nergal-ereshkigal.pasajes.0.not: The El-Amarna version, like Adapa, is preserved in Egypt, where it was used to teach Akkadian. Rogers did not know the Sultantepe version (published by Gurney in 1960), much longer and with an erotic and humorous tone. The "tablet of wisdom" is read today as the tablet of power or of the destinies of the Underworld. The myth explains how Nergal, god of plague and war, became king of the dead alongside Ereshkigal.
t.textos.nergal-ereshkigal.pasajes.0.lec: The Sultantepe version gives Ereshkigal a voice: loneliness, sexual desire and the complaint that she has never known the games of young girls. Gender readings see it as one of the few expressions of female desire in Akkadian literature, although the ending reintegrates the goddess into a scheme of power shared with a male king.
Synthesis; see Rivkah Harris, Gender and Aging in Mesopotamia, 2000, and the introduction by Ponchia and Luukko, SAACT 8, 2013
